food.text: Dates were a staple food across Mesopotamia and the Levant, eaten fresh or dried as a sweet snack. Dried dates were especially valued because they contained 63 to 64 percent sugar by mass, making them a rich source of energy.

In the early 19th century, Damascus was known for its shady cafes lining the banks of the Barada River. This riverside cafe scene was notable enough that the artist William Henry Bartlett published a depiction of it in 1836.

Aleppo's economy, built for centuries on long-distance caravan trade linking the Mediterranean to Mesopotamia, was badly hit when the Suez Canal opened in 1869. Merchants in the city responded by shifting their focus toward more regional trade in wool and agricultural products.

People in the region ate dried dates on their own or stuffed them with fillings such as almonds, walnuts, or tahini. The fruit was also processed into a syrup called dibs, prized as a natural sweetener.

Beyond eating dates fresh, dried, or stuffed, people preserved the fruit by turning it into vinegar, a traditional product of the Middle East made from dates. This vinegar was one of several processed forms of the fruit, alongside pastes and syrups like dibs.

As part of this shift toward regional trade, Aleppo set up one of the Ottoman Empire's first mixed commercial tribunals, called the ticaret mahkamesi, around 1855. The tribunal helped oversee the city's growing trade in goods such as wool and agricultural products.

art.text: In 1899 Robert Koldewey's team unearthed Babylon's central Processional street, giving the modern world its first look at the site. With support from the German Oriental Society, he directed the excavation through 1914. More than 200 people worked there daily, year round, for fifteen years.

Robert Koldewey's excavations at Babylon found two palaces of King Nebuchadnezzar as well as the Ishtar Gate. Claudius Rich and most other 19th-century visitors had thought a mound at Babylon was a royal palace, and Koldewey's work eventually confirmed it.

Claudius Rich, British resident of Baghdad and a self-taught historian, was intrigued by Babylon and researched it personally. His topographical records of the ruins were the first ever published, in 1815, and were reprinted in England no fewer than three times.

Before Babylon, Robert Koldewey had worked for the Royal Museum of Berlin, excavating at Surghul, ancient Nina, and Al-hiba, ancient Lagash, in 1887. His part in the excavation of Babylon began in 1899.

Robert Koldewey developed several modern archaeological techniques, including a method to identify and excavate mud brick architecture. This proved especially useful in excavating the Hanging Gardens of Babylon, which were built about 580 BC using mainly unfired mudbricks.
Koldewey's expedition at Babylon also found the outer walls, inner walls and foundation of Etemenanki, a temple sometimes identified as the Tower of Babel. It also unearthed Nebuchadnezzar's palaces.
The original Ishtar Gate's foundations extended 14 metres underground. During Robert Koldewey's excavation, 14 m of the gate's foundation was uncovered.

war.text: The Mesopotamian campaign was fought between the British Empire and the Central Powers, primarily the Ottoman Empire, over control of Ottoman Iraq. The British side included troops from Britain and Australia, but the vast majority came from the British Raj.
The Mesopotamian campaign began with the British Fao Landing in 1914. The landing was meant to protect Anglo-Persian Oil Company oil fields in Khuzestan province and the Shatt al-Arab waterway.

The Middle Eastern theatre of World War I began on 30 October 1914. It had four main campaigns: Sinai and Palestine, Mesopotamian, Caucasus, and Gallipoli. Four more minor campaigns were fought in Persia, South Arabia, the Arabian interior, and Libya.
war.source_title: Middle Eastern theatre of World War I

war.text: In 1801 and 1802, the Saudis under Abdul Aziz ibn Muhammad ibn Saud attacked and captured the Shia holy cities of Karbala and Najaf in today's Iraq. They massacred parts of the Shia population and destroyed the tomb of Husayn ibn Ali, grandson of Muhammad.
war.source_title: Destruction of early Islamic heritage sites in Saudi Arabia
tags: Abdul Aziz ibn Muhammad ibn Saud

war.text: On 14 November 1914 the Ottoman government declared a holy war, the jihad, against enemies of Islam, with the exception of the Central Powers. This swayed some Ottoman Arabs to stay loyal and fight the Allied Powers, notably including some Shia Muslims, a previously oppressed group within the empire.

A 1912 agreement between the Indian and British military offices made the Indian military responsible for any campaign in the Persian Gulf or Mesopotamia. London saw the Suez Canal and Western Front as more important, whereas Delhi planned an offensive to take Baghdad.

In the middle of the 19th century, wars between the Kurdish Buhti amirs and the Turks led the Kurds to kill many Christians in the Siirt area. This violence against Christians changed the demographics of Upper Mesopotamia.

The Ottoman Empire made a secret German–Ottoman alliance on 2 August 1914. On 6 September 1914 Bronsart von Schellendorf completed a plan in which the Fourth Army would attack Egypt and the Third Army would launch an offensive against the Russians in Eastern Anatolia.
war.source_title: Middle Eastern theatre of World War I

war.text: Before the Ottoman Empire entered the war in 1914, its four armies were split into corps and divisions. Each division had three infantry regiments and an artillery regiment. The First Army had fifteen divisions, while the Fourth Army had only four.
war.source_title: Middle Eastern theatre of World War I

literature.text: In 1815 Lord Byron published "We sat down and wept by the waters", a versified paraphrase of Psalm 137, in his Hebrew Melodies. The psalm is a communal lament about remembering Zion and yearning for Jerusalem during the Babylonian captivity. It ends with prophetic predictions of violent revenge, a call for violence against children, and settings and hymns often omit those final verses.

The psalm about exile in Babylon inspired the famous slave chorus "Va, pensiero" in Verdi's opera Nabucco, first staged in 1842. The chorus grew from the psalm that begins "By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down". The psalm itself expresses hatred for Jerusalem's enemies in violent imagery and ends with a call for violence against children, verses that musical settings often omit.

Excavations in Central and Lower Mesopotamia have been going on since the 19th century, at sites such as Girsu, Eshnunna, Khafajah and Ur. They yielded cuneiform texts and many other important artifacts, which made this area better known than its neighbours.

Byron's paraphrase of Psalm 137 travelled beyond English. It was translated into French by Alexis Paulin Paris and into German by Adolf Böttger. Isaac Nathan had already set the poetry to music in 1815.
Franz Theremin made a German translation of Psalm 137 called "An Babylons Wassern gefangen". Carl Loewe set it to music in 1823 as No. 2 of his Hebräische Gesänge, Op. 4.
Charles-Valentin Alkan wrote a piano piece called Super flumina Babylonis: Paraphrase, Op. 52, in 1859. In the printed score it is preceded by a French translation of Psalm 137.

In 1861 Charles Gounod set "Près du fleuve étranger", a French paraphrase of Psalm 137. In 1866 the setting was published with an English text by Henry Farnie, titled "By Babylon's wave: Psalm CXXXVII".

In 1884 Ferruccio Busoni set another German translation of Byron's poem, "An Babylons Wassern wir weinten". It appeared in his Zwei hebräische Melodien von Lord Byron, BV 202, so Byron's paraphrase was still inspiring new works seventy years later.

science.text: The Hejaz railway, ordered by Sultan Abdul Hamid II in March 1900, ran from Damascus to Medina. It was the only railway completely built and operated by the Ottoman Empire. Its main aim was to link Istanbul with the holy cities of Arabia.

Western interest in Babylon grew in the 19th century, especially after cuneiform was deciphered in the mid-1800s. Scholars could now read ancient Mesopotamian texts for themselves. Expeditions such as those of Austen Henry Layard and Robert Koldewey added to what was known about the region's ancient civilizations.

On January 23, 1862, missionary W. M. Thomson proposed a college of higher learning that would include medical training, to be built in Beirut with Daniel Bliss as its president. The college opened its doors on December 3, 1866, with a class of only sixteen students.

In 1903, Germany began building the Berlin-Baghdad railway, a roughly 1,600-kilometre line meant to link Berlin to Baghdad through what is now Turkey, Syria and Iraq. German planners hoped it would give them access to a Persian Gulf port and to suspected oil fields in Mesopotamia.

In the Hilla region of Ottoman Iraq, the Hilla branch of the Euphrates began silting up during the nineteenth century, causing much farmland to be lost to drought. Engineers reversed this in 1911 to 1913 by building the Hindiya Barrage, which diverted water from the deeper Hindiya branch of the Euphrates back into the Hilla canal.

Layard published Nineveh and Its Remains in 1849. The book introduced the Western world to Assyrian and Babylonian civilization. He is best known for his excavations at Nineveh, the ancient capital of the Neo-Assyrian Empire.

Construction of the American University of Beirut's campus began with College Hall, which took two years to build. It was completed in 1873, the same year the campus's first medical building was also put into use.

Daniel Bliss, an American missionary born in Vermont, arrived in Lebanon in 1856 and spent years running small schools in Aley and Souk-al-Gharb while studying Arabic. His work convinced the Syrian mission to open a new college, which he had chartered in New York in 1863 and which opened in Beirut in 1866.

Funding and engineering for the Berlin-Baghdad railway came mainly from the German Empire through Deutsche Bank and the Philipp Holzmann company, which had already built the Anatolian Railway linking Istanbul, Ankara and Konya in the 1890s. By the outbreak of the First World War, the line was still about 960 kilometres short of reaching Baghdad.

German engineers built Aleppo's Baghdad railway station in 1912 as part of the Berlin-Baghdad railway project, and the very first train from the station traveled to the town of Jarabulus. By the start of the First World War the railway had reached Aleppo, with a branch line extending to Tripoli in Lebanon.

In 1913, a dedicated railway station opened in central Damascus to serve as the starting point of the Hejaz line. This came just a year before the outbreak of World War I halted further construction of the railway toward Mecca.

Engineering courses were first offered at the American University of Beirut starting in 1913, decades before a separate School of Engineering was created there in 1951. This made engineering one of the college's later academic additions, arriving nearly half a century after its founding in 1866.

politics.text: In 1831 Muhammad Ali Pasha, the Ottoman governor of Egypt, sent his son Ibrahim Pasha to conquer Ottoman Syria, a reward he felt he was owed for helping Sultan Mahmud II fight the Greek War of Independence. By 1832 Ibrahim's army controlled Damascus, Aleppo and much of Syria.

In February 1840, an Italian monk, Father Thomas, and his Muslim servant, Ibrahim Amrah, disappeared in Damascus's Jewish quarter, setting off the Damascus affair. The Jewish community was accused of murdering them and draining their blood to bake matzo, a blood libel. Egyptian authorities, backed by the French consul, tortured a large number of Jews until they "confessed" to the murder, and it is believed that some prisoners died during their interrogation.
Ibrahim Pasha's Egyptian army besieged the port of Acre for six months before it fell in May 1832. He then swept on to capture Aleppo, Homs, Beirut, Sidon, Tripoli and Damascus.

The Second Egyptian-Ottoman War, which lasted into 1841, saw the Convention of Alexandria agreed on 27 November 1840. Muhammad Ali gave up his claims to Syria and returned the Ottoman fleet, and in exchange he and his sons were recognized as Egypt's only legitimate rulers.

French consul Ulysse de Ratti-Menton, described by historians as antisemitic, ordered an investigation of the Jewish quarter after the monk's disappearance and encouraged the Egyptian governor Sharif Pasha to act. A Jewish barber called Negrin confessed under torture to killing Father Thomas with seven other notable Jewish men. Those men were also tortured, and five of the seven confessed to the murder of the monk and his servant. Authorities then seized sixty-three Jewish children as hostages until their mothers revealed where the blood was, and it is believed some prisoners died under interrogation.

The Berlin–Baghdad railway, begun in 1903, was funded mainly by the German Empire through Deutsche Bank. Its goal was to link Berlin with Ottoman Baghdad and reach a port on the Persian Gulf, deepening Germany's ties to Ottoman Mesopotamia.

In 1839, Sir Moses Montefiore visited Muhammad Ali in Egypt and proposed a large-scale scheme to resettle Jews and regenerate Palestine, which Muhammad Ali accepted. The plan stalled when Muhammad Ali was forced to withdraw from Palestine, which returned to Turkish rule.

The Damascus affair set off attacks on Jews by Muslims and Christians alike, and a mob pillaged the synagogue in the suburb of Jobar and destroyed its scrolls of the Law. It drew international protest from Jewish leaders such as Sir Moses Montefiore of Britain and Adolphe Crémieux of France. Muhammad Ali released the prisoners who had survived but refused to acquit them. Only in November 1840, after Egyptian withdrawal and the restoration of Ottoman Syria, did Sultan Abdulmejid I decree that all charges be dropped.

By the late 1800s, debts from wars like the Russo-Turkish War of 1877-78 left Ottoman finances under the control of the Ottoman Public Debt Administration, which answered to the Great Powers. This weakness let Germany push economic projects such as the Baghdad railway into Ottoman Mesopotamia.

When Aleppo's Baghdad railway station opened in 1912 as part of the German-built Berlin–Baghdad line, its very first train departed for the town of Jarabulus. The station, also called Gare de Bagdad, was the main station of the city of Aleppo.

Although Germany wanted the railway to reach the Persian Gulf, the British made sure that the final stretch linking Baghdad to the port of Basra was reserved for them rather than the Germans. The full line to Baghdad was in fact not finished until 1940, well after the outbreak of the First World War.

philosophy.text: In 1853 the Free Church of Scotland theologian Alexander Hislop published a pamphlet that grew into The Two Babylons. It argued that the Catholic Church was the Babylon of the Apocalypse described in the Bible. He tried to trace Catholic practices back to ancient Babylonian religion.

In 1899 the English Assyriologist L. W. King wrote Babylonian Religion and Mythology. The book analyzes the religious system of ancient Babylon and its link to the myths that shaped how Babylonians understood their world. It also examines the psychism and thought processes of the Babylonian people.

Hislop leaned heavily on Austen Henry Layard's publications about his excavations at Nineveh, which had only just been discovered in 1851. This gave the book an appearance of careful research. Hislop cited Layard's find of Astarte's Assyrian name, Ishtar, and took it to be identical to the word Easter.

In 1898 Morris Jastrow Jr. published The Religion of Babylonia and Assyria. Drawing on cuneiform texts, it explores gods such as Marduk, Ishtar and Enlil, along with temple worship, sacrifices and divination. Jastrow links these beliefs to daily life, political structures and the ethical views of these ancient civilizations.

Hislop built on the Panbabylonian school of Hyperdiffusionism, which was common in the 19th century. He argued that the mystery religions of Late Antiquity were offshoots of one ancient religion founded at the Tower of Babel. Twentieth-century scholars have since relegated Panbabylonism to pseudohistory.

The Two Babylons was expanded in 1858 and went through many editions. A 3rd edition appeared in 1862 and a 7th in 1871, only six years after Hislop's death in 1865. A popular edition followed in 1903.

Theophilus G. Pinches wrote a detailed 1906 work titled The Religion of Babylonia and Assyria. Although many deities' names are now read differently, it is described as a classic. It belongs to the wave of scholarship on Babylonian religion that followed the 19th-century recovery of the region's texts.
tags: The Religion of Babylonia and Assyria

culture.text: Western interest in Babylon began to grow in the 19th century, especially after cuneiform was deciphered in the mid-1800s. Scholars could then read ancient Mesopotamian texts for themselves. Early expeditions by Austen Henry Layard and Robert Koldewey added to what people knew of these civilizations.

In 1853 the Scottish theologian Alexander Hislop published The Two Babylons, which began as a religious pamphlet. It argued that Catholic holidays such as Christmas and Easter could be traced back to pagan festivals. Hislop claimed the Catholic Church was the Whore of Babylon of the Book of Revelation.

Before Levantine archaeology emerged in the late 19th and early 20th century, knowledge of Canaanite religion came mostly from the Hebrew Bible. It was supplemented by a few Greek sources, such as Lucian's On the Syrian Goddess. Later archaeological finds have since become the main source.

Claudius Rich, a self-taught historian and British resident of Baghdad, researched Babylon out of personal fascination. His topographical records of the ruins were the first ever published, in 1815. They were reprinted in England no fewer than three times.

The German archaeologist Robert Koldewey began his part in the excavation of Babylon in 1899. He led the dig at the Ishtar Gate site from 1904 to 1914. His work eventually uncovered two palaces of King Nebuchadnezzar along with the gate itself.

Julius Oppert, a French-German Assyriologist, contributed to the early study of Babylon by translating Babylonian legal texts. One of them was the Code of Hammurabi. His work was part of the 19th-century effort to read ancient Mesopotamia's own records.

In 1898 Morris Jastrow Jr. published The Religion of Babylonia and Assyria. It explored the gods, myths and rituals of Babylonian and Assyrian culture, highlighting deities such as Marduk, Ishtar and Enlil. It also covered temple worship, sacrifices and divination.

The American University of Beirut, then still called the Syrian Protestant College, first used Arabic as its language of instruction because it was common to the region's many ethnic groups. In 1887 it switched entirely to English, the language it has used ever since.

Hislop drew on Panbabylonism, a 19th-century school of Hyperdiffusionism that held Classical and Ancient Near Eastern civilization took its inspiration from Babylon. He concluded that the mystery religions of Late Antiquity were offshoots of one religion founded at the Tower of Babel. Twentieth-century scholars have since relegated Panbabylonism to pseudohistory.

Hislop asserted that the Catholic Church was the Whore of Babylon of the Book of Revelation, and that "the Pope himself is truly and properly the lineal representative of Belshazzar." He claimed that the Christogram IHS, the first three Greek letters in the name of Jesus, represented Latin characters standing for Isis, Horus and Seb. These were among his attempts to trace Catholic doctrines back to the worship of Nimrod.
